title: Single vineyards
subtitle: Rioja's new map
objectives: Name key producers of the movement

steps.title: Viñedo Singular
steps.body: In 2017, Rioja created Viñedo Singular, single vineyard, for wines from specific, registered plots. Rules include vines at least 35 years old, low yields, hand harvesting and tasting approval. It aims to recognise the best sites, as in Burgundy. Labels can also name a village, Vino de Municipio, or a zone, Vino de Zona.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: For a century, Rioja focused on ageing and blending, not site. Producers like Remírez de Ganuza, Artadi, Contino and Telmo Rodríguez pushed for place-based classification. Some, like Artadi, left the DOCa in 2015 in protest before the new rules. The debate continues about how far Rioja should go towards a Burgundian model.

steps.prompt: Which is a requirement for Viñedo Singular?
steps.explanation: Old vines, low yields and hand harvesting are required.

steps.title: Old classics
steps.body: Some historic Rioja wines were single vineyard long before the rules: Viña Tondonia, from López de Heredia, since 1913; Contino, the first single-estate Rioja in the 1970s. These show that site has always mattered, even under the blending tradition.

steps.prompt: Which are Rioja's place-based label categories?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Viñedo Singular, since 2017, names single vineyards
Village and zone wines show place
Historic wines like Viña Tondonia were early single vineyards
